articles.body:
Tennessee Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn on Tuesday released a video appearing to use artificial intelligence to have her resemble rapper Kendrick Lamar during his 2025 Super Bowl LIX Halftime Show performance.

The video depicts Blackburn, who is running for governor , on a football field, backed up by Rep. Tim Burchett (R-Tenn.), Sen. Bill Hagerty (R-Tenn.), state Sen. Brent Taylor (R) and WWE professional wrestler Kane. The wrestler, whose real name is Glenn Thomas Jacobs, served as the mayor of Knox County, Tenn., until last September.

Blackburn is seen in the video singing into a microphone, with Lamar’s “Not Like Us” playing in the background. Lamar played the song, a dis track against fellow rapper Drake, during the halftime show in 2025.

Blackburn posted the video to the social platform X, with the caption: “Tomorrow. Ready to roll.”

Comments on the post slammed the video, with some calling it “ AI slop ” while others urged Blackburn to take the video down .

Another comment reacted to the video with a photo of Sen. Katie Britt’s (R-Ala.) reaction after Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.) and his staff appeared to mix up the Iowa Hawkeyes with the Atlanta Hawks during former special counsel Jack Smith’s testimony before the Senate Judiciary Committee late last month.

“When I say please stop using AI to support our campaign, this is what I mean,” Blackburn’s Democratic gubernatorial opponent, Jerri Green, wrote on X in response to the video.

Lamar has not publicly reacted to Blackburn’s video, nor have his representatives released a statement.

Blackburn has spoken out against the use of deepfakes made with AI without licensing or approval after musical artists approached lawmakers in May 2025. She and Sens. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.), Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) and Chris Coons (D-Del.) introduced the No Fakes Act to protect the voice and visual likenesses of individuals and creators from being used without permission.

“This is something that would provide that extra protection for these creators, so whether it’s copying their voice or copying their works, they have a legal standing and a right to defend themself and their creation,” Blackburn said during a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on intellectual property in November 2024.

A version of the No Fakes Act was introduced in May and forwarded to the Senate Judiciary Committee.

Lamar notably used deepfake technology for the music video for his 2022 song “The Heart Part 5,” part of his “Mr. Morale & the Big Steppers” album.

Throughout the video, Lamar morphs from O.J. Simpson to Ye, the artist formerly known as Kanye West, then to actors Jussie Smollett and Will Smith, before changing into the late Los Angeles Lakers star Kobe Bryant and the late Los Angeles rapper Nipsey Hussle. The song’s lyrics correspond with each face and were intended to be from their perspectives.

articles.title: Sleeper GOP candidate puts blue-leaning state in play as fraud scandal shadows Dems
articles.summary: Michele Tafoya trails Peggy Flanagan by just four points as Minnesota's massive welfare fraud scandal reshapes the rare GOP Senate pickup bid.
articles.body: Republicans are eyeing a rare Senate pickup opportunity in Minnesota, where GOP nominee Michele Tafoya is narrowing the gap with Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, prompting Fox News to move the race toward Republicans less than three weeks before Election Day. It's been nearly a quarter-century since Republicans last won a Senate election in the blue-leaning state. But Tafoya, a former longtime NFL sideline reporter, is aiming to break that losing streak by flipping the seat held by retiring Democratic Sen. Tina Smith. A new Minnesota Star Tribune/KARE 11 poll shows Tafoya trailing Flanagan by just four percentage points. On Tuesday, the Fox News Power Rankings shifted the race to the right, from Likely Democrat to Lean Democrat. GOP SENATE HOPEFUL SOUNDS ALARM AFTER TERROR PLOT THWARTED "The more that Minnesotans learn about me and my opponent and see what my opponent has failed to do over the last eight years alongside [Democratic Gov.] Tim Walz, they're understanding Minnesota needs change. We need fresh ideas, we need an independent thinker and they're jumping on board," Tafoya said in a Fox News Digital interview. Fox News Digital reached out to the Flanagan campaign for comment but didn't receive a response at the time this story was published. The race is unfolding against the backdrop of Minnesota's massive welfare assistance fraud scandal, which has attracted national attention for nearly a year and prompted Democratic Gov. Tim Walz to abandon his 2026 re-election bid. The scandal has also become a central issue in Tafoya's campaign against Flanagan. Tafoya noted that "there has been historic fraud under this administration, where Peggy Flanagan, my opponent, has been the second-in-charge in this state. And not only was the money stolen, it hollowed out these programs that were supposed to be getting help, like kids' meals or autistic kids or seniors who were supposed to be getting visits, health visits, wellness visits. And, so, that's been hollowed out. DEMS SEE NEW CHANCES TO FLIP SENATE SEATS BUT GOP'S MASSIVE CASH ADVANTAGE AN OBSTACLE "Walz understood that he was not going to win another term as governor with these conditions, but my opponent thinks she deserves a promotion. I think people are starting to realize she deserves a pink slip." Flanagan has said she is "incredibly angry with the fraud," has acknowledged public frustration over the scandal and said more could have been done sooner to catch and prevent the fraud. The lieutenant governor has noted that she was not in charge of the state agencies at the center of the scandals or steering the daily state response. She has also distanced herself from Walz, who has accepted blame for the fraud. DEMOCRATS THINK A BLUE WAVE IS BUILDING - HERE ARE THREE FACTORS THAT COULD STOP IT "It's wall-to-wall coverage on every nightly news program here for months and months. We're seeing it in polling," Minnesota-based veteran national Republican strategist Kirsten Kukowski told Fox News Digital. Pointing to Flanagan, Kukowski said she has "a lot of fraud baggage ... and it's really made the Senate race really tight here." Tafoya is also highlighting a recent spate of gang-related shootings in the Minneapolis-St. Paul suburbs and on Monday announced a five-point-plan to combat the violence. "We will do more in our first eight weeks as a U.S. Senator than Peggy Flanagan has done in eight years as the second in charge," she told Fox News Digital. WHO'S UP AND WHO'S DOWN IN THE LATEST FOX NEWS MIDTERM POWER RANKINGS "First of all, we've got to name the problem, and even Somali lawmakers and law enforcement have named this problem. We have a Somali gang violence problem. We've got to name it. She refuses to name it. You can't fix it if you don't name it," Tafoya emphasized as she referred to Flanagan. Flanagan, a progressive candidate backed by left-wing champions, Sens. Bernie Sanders Elizabeth Warren and Rep. Ro Khanna, topped more moderate Democratic Rep. Angie Craig by roughly 20 points in the August Senate primary. Tafoya grabbed over 50% of the vote in the GOP Senate primary as she topped a crowded field of rivals. She was heavily recruited by national Republicans, including Sen. Tim Scott, the National Republican Senatorial Committee chair. "We did a really good job of recruiting the most independent-minded Republican who understands why it's important to win in Minnesota," Scott said in an interview on Fox News' "Hannity." "Michele Tafoya has a story to tell. She's doing a really good job. This is a race that will come down to the wire." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Senate Majority Leader John Thune, the top Republican in the chamber, recently teamed up on the campaign trail in Minnesota with Tafoya. But the Thune-aligned Senate Leadership Fund, the top super PAC backing GOP Senate candidates, has yet to make a major investment in the race. Asked about national Republican support, Tafoya said, "We are getting small dollar donations from all over the country. We're getting donations from every county in this state, and I am a happy warrior. And I will deal with the circumstances I'm given. ... We're going to win this campaign on ideas." Democrats are hopeful that popular Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar, who is running for governor this year, may help push Flanagan over the finish line. "Our latest poll has Flanagan with a strong lead, and we fully expect her to be elected to the U.S. Senate," Lauren French, communications director for the Senate Democrat-aligned Senate Majority PAC, told Fox News Digital. French argued that "Republicans are spending in deep red states and watching the battleground map extend around them. Their desperate last-minute attempt to push Minnesota into play is a political ploy." DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB Flanagan has repeatedly tied Tafoya to President Donald Trump, whose approval ratings are well underwater in Minnesota. "Michele Tafoya is all in for Donald Trump — and he's all in for her," Flanagan reiterated Monday in a social media post. Flanagan, who is Native American, also wrote on X, "My Ojibwe name is Gizhiiwewidamookwe, which means ‘Speaks in a Loud and Clear Voice Woman.’ I’m going to be Minnesota’s voice in the U.S. Senate — not Donald Trump’s." But Tafoya appears to be putting some daylight between herself and Trump, as she highlights her support for abortion rights. "I’m a pro-choice Republican not afraid to stand up to my party," Tafoya says in a new campaign commercial. "When Trump is right, I will work with him. When he is wrong, I will stand up for Minnesota." The ad was quickly criticized by leaders on the right. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Among them was Mercedes Schlapp, a senior fellow at the Conservative Political Action Conference, who said on social media, "Pro-life Republicans will stay home after watching this ad." But hours later, Trump gave Tafoya a plug, telling the crowd at an Ohio rally he headlined, "You have to vote for Michele Tafoya, who’s a very respected person."

articles.title: GOP Sen. Tillis asks Musk to explain Ukraine losing access to Starlink
articles.summary: Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) is pressing Elon Musk to explain Ukraine’s loss of military access to Starlink and expressing hope that Ukraine’s restricted access to the space-based communications network was because of an error and not a deliberate decision. Tillis called on Musk in a social media post to “please tell me these overnight disruptions…
articles.body:
Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) is pressing Elon Musk to explain Ukraine’s loss of military access to Starlink and expressing hope that Ukraine’s restricted access to the space-based communications network was because of an error and not a deliberate decision.

Tillis called on Musk in a social media post to “please tell me these overnight disruptions to Starlink terminals in Ukraine were unintended — that @SpaceX is doing everything it can to fix a temporary glitch.”

Tillis warned that “intentionally degrading Ukraine’s ability to defend itself might be construed as aiding and abetting a mass murder,” referring to Russian President Vladimir Putin.

“Can you confirm that’s not SpaceX’s intent?” he added.

“Supporting Ukrainian sovereignty — or at the very least, allowing for it — should not be a gray area for the U.S. government or for American corporations. Can you clarify the SpaceX position?” Tillis posted on social platform X.

Musk is the founder and CEO of SpaceX, which owns Starlink.

Ukraine said Wednesday that its military lost access to the military version of Starlink, which it uses for vital communications, and some Ukrainian officials speculated the decision to restrict its access may have come from Washington.

Ukrainian defense adviser Serhii Beskrestnov said SpaceX imposed speed limits on Starlink’s internet terminals overnight, according to NBC News.

Former Ukraine Minister of Defense Mykhailo Fedorov said Wednesday afternoon that Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160 km per hour was being restored. “Removing Starshield’s speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine’s defense,” Fedorov wrote on X, which Musk also owns.

He thanked Musk for the returned speed and wrote “we hope for your continued support.”

Starlink data speeds were limited to prevent Ukraine from using it for drones, airplanes and helicopters and other objects moving faster than 100 mph, according to a source familiar, which hampered its defenses from intercepting Russian-launched drones.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Wednesday warned the loss of full access to Starlink would cost Ukrainian lives and blasted the limits on the network as a “big mistake.”

“People will die, of course, if attacks will continue and if Starlink will not work … it’s not helpful,” he said.

Zelensky said he hoped the limits on Ukrainian access to the network were a “mistake” or perhaps a “technical problem” at SpaceX.

articles.title: WATCH: Georgia Senate debate erupts over white supremacy allegations, Epstein ties in fiery exchange
articles.summary: Candidates running for the US Senate in Georgia clashed over alleged neo-Nazi activity and ties to Jeffrey Epstein during their last debate before the election.
articles.body: Georgia's contentious U.S. Senate race erupted into a heated confrontation Tuesday night as Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., accused GOP challenger Rep. Mike Collins, R-Ga., of allowing the dissemination of "neo-Nazi propaganda" inside his own home, prompting Collins to fire back over Ossoff's financial support from a billionaire with ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. The exchange unfolded during the candidates' second and final debate ahead of the Nov. 3 general election, which was hosted by the Atlanta Press Club and broadcast by Georgia Public Broadcasting network. During the debate, Ossoff sought to tie his GOP opponent to White nationalism and repeatedly demanded that Collins commit to stopping the dissemination of hateful rhetoric involving his campaign staff, in particular Collins' son-in-law, which Ossoff alleged has continued despite blowback. Meanwhile, Collins accused his Democrat opponent of fueling threats against his family, refusing to return campaign support connected to LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman and questioned Ossoff over his support for candidates linked to controversial streamer Hasan Piker. DEM ‘EPSTEIN CLASS’ ATTACK BACKFIRES AS TOP CANDIDATES FUNDED BY EPSTEIN-TIED BILLIONAIRE "How weak a person do you have to be to be unable to stop someone under your own roof from disseminating neo-Nazi propaganda while you run for the Senate?" Ossoff asked, referencing reporting about his opponent's son-in-law, David Alan Scheer II, who was the subject of a CNN investigation about sharing Nazi propaganda imagery, promoting antisemitic conspiracy theories and polling his online followers about whether he should produce a video titled "Why Gen-Z Doesn't Hate Hitler." "How about this, Mike? We can shake hands on it," Ossoff continued to press. "Will you commit tonight that for the remainder of this campaign, it's just three weeks, Mike, you won't allow any more neo-Nazi propaganda to be produced from your house? Can you make that commitment?" Collins responded by accusing Ossoff of inflaming hostility toward his family, pointing to threats he said he and his son-in-law had received. "I'm a little tired of this, Jon," Collins said. "There's a crazy person in jail right now because of your rhetoric," he alleged, before saying he had received another threat just the previous day. JON OSSOFF SILENT ON SPLC INDICTMENT AFTER TAKING MORE THAN $700K FROM AFFILIATE OF INDICTED GROUP "You have not denounced, you've not condemned Reid Hoffman, one of your largest donors out there, one that's been supporting you with over $1 million," Collins shot back. "Why don't you denounce that? Why don't you return that money?" Collins was referring to Reid Hoffman, the billionaire LinkedIn co-founder and major Democratic donor whose past relationship with Epstein has drawn scrutiny. Hoffman has acknowledged meeting with Epstein after the financier's 2008 conviction for sex offenses and visiting his private island. Hoffman also contributed $7,000 directly to Ossoff's campaign and $1 million to a political action committee supporting the Georgia Democrat, according to previously reported campaign finance records. Earlier in the debate, Collins went further, accusing Hoffman of sending Epstein ice cream with a message referencing girls, while again pressing Ossoff to reject his financial support. "Jon Ossoff, his number one donor, one of his largest donors, is Reid Hoffman, the same guy that's in the same files, the same guy that sent ice cream, ice cream to Jeffrey Epstein on his birthday and said, 'This is for the girls,'" Collins said during an earlier exchange in the debate. THUNE-ALIGNED GROUPS UNLEASH HISTORIC WAR CHEST TO DEFEND SENATE MAJORITY: 'WINNING MESSAGE' The Wall Street Journal previously reported that Hoffman sent Epstein ice cream in 2014 with a message indicating it was intended for him or "for the girls." Hoffman has apologized for his association with Epstein, which he said stemmed from fundraising activities involving the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and has not been accused of wrongdoing in connection with Epstein's crimes. Ossoff rejected the Hoffman comparison, however, arguing that the allegations against Collins involved someone living in the congressman's home rather than a political donor. "Mike, if any of these folks were based in my house, then I'd understand you to ask me to take responsibility for them," Ossoff said. "What I asked you, Mike, was, can you commit for just three weeks to stop the production of neo-Nazi propaganda from your home?" Earlier in the debate, Collins was directly questioned about concerns from Black Georgians over allegations of White-nationalist ties involving members of his political operation. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I condemn any sort of hate speech, antisemitism, hate of any kind. It's abhorrent," Collins responded, adding that he had fired staffers when controversies arose. Collins also sought to turn the accusations back on Ossoff by criticizing his support for Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed and invoking left-wing streamer Hasan Piker, who Collins blasted for saying the U.S. deserved 9/11, and promoting anti-Semitism. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "He hangs his hat on this Abdul El-Sayed, you know, the guy that hates Israel — best friends with Hasan Piker, who said that America deserves 9/11," Collins said Tuesday night. Ossoff has previously condemned Piker's rhetoric, telling The Atlanta Journal-Constitution through a spokesperson that he "unreservedly rejects reckless and dangerous rhetoric" suggesting political advocacy justifies violence against Jewish Americans or any other community.

articles.title: Trump-backed GOP candidate who ousted scandal-plagued incumbent warns against 'never-ending war' with Iran
articles.summary: Television journalist turned congressional hopeful Ryan Elijah says transparency, accountability will be his focus following victory over Cory Mills in contentious Florida GOP primary.
articles.body: For 14 years, Ryan Elijah reported on Central Florida’s biggest stories from the television newsroom. Now, he is on a mission to represent the same community in Congress. Elijah stepped into a contentious GOP primary in which he warned that incumbent Cory Mills was at risk of losing the Republican-leaning district to the Democrats, following a series of personal and professional scandals. Elijah won a convincing victory in the August 18 Republican primary, receiving 47% of the vote to Mills' 34%. Trump, who had originally endorsed Mills, later claimed that he had privately encouraged the embattled congressman to withdraw from the race. REP CORY MILLS DRAWS FIRST REPUBLICAN CHALLENGER AS SEXUAL MISCONDUCT ALLEGATIONS, EXPULSION THREAT MOUNT Recently, the veteran television journalist sat down with Fox News Digital to discuss his views on Iran, affordability, and immigration, while pledging to remain an independent voice in Congress, and a strong advocate for Volusia and Seminole counties. Elijah did not take the decision to leave working in media lightly, but felt a call to leadership: "I love my job. It's something I could have retired from TV and been perfectly happy. But I think we all look for the time you're asked to step up and lead. And for me, that was this time. When we saw how the primary was playing out, it just became clear that we were going to lose this election in November. "And I decided that we had the connections in this community to throw our hat in the ring. We had the trust from the community and the primary played out a lot like we thought it would, where people wanted a choice. I think that's what primaries are all about in Seminole County and Volusia County spoke really loud. In that primary, and now I think they put us in a great spot to hold this seat in November." Elijah pledges to put transparency and accountability front and center for the constituents of the seventh district: "Well, I think transparency and accountability are huge issues. I think when I talk to people, they don't feel like they're heard very much in Washington. And I think that you have to be transparent about whatever you can. And first of all, if you have nothing to hide, that's the best way to be transparent because you can exactly show your business dealings and how your life dealings are. "And that's something we've talked about a lot…and then in terms of accountability, no one is above the law. And that's a message that Americans want to hear, whether you're a Democrat or Republican, there are laws for a reason, and we have to make sure those laws are upheld." As the military engagement with Iran is rattling global energy markets and pinching Americans' pocketbooks, Elijah concedes the need to thwart a nuclear Iran, but also is wary of another forever war: GOP RISING STAR HELPED TOPPLE TRUMP-BACKED INCUMBENT. NOW HE'S CAUGHT LEADERSHIP'S EYE "This is a decade-long issue and a conflict between Iran and its proxies, where they have targeted and they have killed Americans. So the U.S. military right now is trying to end that conflict. But as representatives, we have to listen to the American people. We have to listen to central Floridians. "And they have been very clear on this. They're concerned about it. They are concerned this is going to be a never-ending war. They don't want that. I don't want that either. I share that belief, which is why I think we need to draw this conflict down. And we need to make sure that Iran is not a nuclear threat." On the immigration issue, Elijah cites improvement under GOP leadership on the issue, but argues that enforcement focus should remain on criminals: "This is another issue where I think you have to look at where we've come from. When you let tens of millions of illegal people into this country, you're going to have issues that take a long time to fix. And I think if you look at the way there has to be a federal, a local, and a state cooperation with immigration, that's what it takes to work. Which is why when I talk to all the sheriffs in our district that are endorsing us, they're handling immigration much better than other parts around the country because they have that cooperation. "We need to start with the criminals. We have got many criminals still here illegally in the United States. That's what they focused on in central Florida. That's what ICE needs to focus on, removing the criminals. And there's a compassionate way to handle this as we've got an issue that is not going to be fixed in just six or 12 months." Elijah consistently emphasizes that he will be an independent voice for the district, not a partisan rubber stamp: "Well, I've said a lot. Look, I ran in this primary without the president's endorsement. I've been an independent voice in this and I've told a lot of people that ask me that question. "As you can imagine, I go to a lot of doors. That's a question: ‘Will you support the president? Will you not support the president?’ And what I tell them is, if it's a policy that supports our country and supports our district, I'm going to support that policy. "More often than not, I will because I'm a Republican. I like a lot of those policies. If there's a policy I disagree with, we won't. So in that situation, that's where things are at." Finally, Elijah acknowledges that affordability, while lacking a quick and easy fix, is the defining 2026 issue for much of the electorate: "I think the number one thing that we hear from people, and that's affordability, and that's not an easy fix, but I think what they want out of government is accountability. We talked about that before, that government is going to be accountable on its spending, on its policies, and getting inflation down, which is going to lower interest rates. It's going to lower the cost of living. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "People in Central Florida, people around the country, they want to be heard. And what they're saying in a very clear tone right now is make sure that you control government spending and protect the future of our children. That's probably the biggest thing I want them to notice." Elijah will be facing Navy veteran and former NASA employee Bale Dalton in the November 3 general election.

articles.title: White House confirms appeal as Trump-appointed judge extends ruling restoring CNN, MS NOW, Politico access
articles.summary: Judge Timothy Kelly found Trump's ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters likely violated the First Amendment. The White House vows to appeal.
articles.body: A federal judge appointed by President Donald Trump extended an order blocking the administration from banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters from the White House, finding the restrictions likely violated the outlets' First Amendment rights. U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly issued a preliminary injunction Tuesday night, allowing journalists from the three organizations to retain their White House press credentials while their lawsuit proceeds, according to The Associated Press. A White House official confirmed to Fox News Digital that the administration intends to appeal the ruling, criticizing the decision and defending the restrictions on the outlets' access to the president. MAMDANI TELLS TRUMP BANNED WHITE HOUSE OUTLETS ARE WELCOME AT NYC MEETING "The fake news has no place demanding a spot in the president’s Oval Office. The lies they smear are a disservice to the American public and tear at the very fabric of our democracy. They’re completely capable of reporting from directly outside. We intend to appeal this misguided decision," the official said. Theodore Boutrous Jr., an attorney representing CNN, MS NOW and Politico, welcomed the ruling in a statement provided to Fox News Digital. "We are grateful that the court ruled in favor of our clients CNN, MS NOW and POLITICO and secured access to the White House for these news media organizations and their journalists," the statement read. Boutrous accused Trump of restricting the outlets' access to punish unfavorable reporting and said the ruling protects the organizations' constitutional rights. The ruling expands Kelly's Sept. 24 temporary restraining order, which found the outlets were likely to succeed on their Fifth Amendment due process claims. Kelly now also determined the restrictions likely violated the First Amendment because they were motivated by Trump's objections to the outlets' coverage rather than national security concerns, the AP reported. Kelly also rejected the administration's request to suspend his ruling pending an appeal, according to the AP. WHITE HOUSE TV POOL TO SUSPEND COVERAGE OF TRUMP EVENTS Trump announced the ban in September, criticizing the three organizations' reporting. White House officials subsequently deactivated or confiscated reporters' credentials, prompting the outlets and three journalists to sue over alleged First Amendment and Fifth Amendment violations. Justice Department attorneys argued that White House press access is a privilege, not a right, and defended the president's authority to determine which journalists receive credentials. Fox News Digital reached out to the Justice Department for comment. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The lawsuit remains pending, with the preliminary injunction keeping the three outlets' White House credentials in place while the legal battle continues. Fox News Digital's Michael Sinkewicz and the Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Karen Bass apologizes for Palisades Fire during LA mayor debate
articles.summary: Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass expressed regret for being away from her city during the massive January 2025 wildfires in Southern California, apologizing to voters for her absence while debating her mayoral race opponent Tuesday night. “Let me just say that I am so profoundly sorry that I was not in my city when my…
articles.body:
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass expressed regret for being away from her city during the massive January 2025 wildfires in Southern California, apologizing to voters for her absence while debating her mayoral race opponent Tuesday night.

“Let me just say that I am so profoundly sorry that I was not in my city when my city needed me,” Bass said during the debate, which was moderated by NBC4 Los Angeles and Telemundo 52. “There’s not a day that goes by that I don’t think of the lives lost, the families that lost their homes, or the families where the home is still standing but they’re not able to be in it.”

Bass was reportedly on her way back to Los Angeles after she was part of a U.S. delegation to Accra, Ghana, for the inauguration of Ghanaian President John Mahama. Los Angeles’s Emergency Management Department reportedly warned the mayor’s aides about the fire risk ahead of her trip, according to the Los Angeles Times .

Bass’s challenger, City Council member Nithya Raman, accused the incumbent of being “missing in action” during the January 2025 fires, as well as another this June. The absences prompted “a crisis of trust” toward City Hall, she said.

“The question that I heard over and over … across the entire city was, ‘Where is our mayor? Where is our mayor?'” Raman said. “If there is another emergency, you will not have to ask — if I am mayor — where our mayor is. I will be on the front lines.”

Frustration with Bass’s handling of the fires drove many voters to support former reality TV star Spencer Pratt in the primary. Pratt lost his home in the Palisades Fire.

Bass has pushed back on criticism of her handling of the Palisades Fire and the corresponding Eaton Fire. Pratt emphasized Bass’s role during the fires as part of his campaign, and polling from the University of California, Berkeley, released last month showed 56 percent of Angelenos thought Bass did a “poor” or “very poor” job responding to the devastation.

That same poll showed Raman leading Bass 39 percent to 28 percent, with 33 percent of likely voters still undecided.

Both fires burned more than 38,000 acres and destroyed more than 16,000 structures across Southern California, according to the state’s Office of Emergency Services.

The fires killed 31 people, making it the second-deadliest wildfire in California history behind the 2018 Camp fire, which had a death toll of 85, KTLA reported in January.

Former President Biden was temporarily stuck in Los Angeles because of the fires ahead of a trip to the Coachella Valley to designate a new monument, CNN and local independent outlet L.A. Taco reported at the time. The fires altered his plans, and he received a briefing from Santa Monica officials before flying to Washington later in the day.

articles.title: GOP rep warns that Trump’s agenda is ‘dead’ unless he reverses course on Ukraine
articles.summary: A prominent House Republican warned Wednesday that President Trump’s legislative wish list will be “dead” on Capitol Hill during the lame-duck session unless the administration reverses recent moves that could help Russia in its war with Ukraine. Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.), an Air Force veteran who sometimes spars with the White House on foreign policy,…
articles.body:
A prominent House Republican warned Wednesday that President Trump’s legislative wish list will be “dead” on Capitol Hill during the lame-duck session unless the administration reverses recent moves that could help Russia in its war with Ukraine.

Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.), an Air Force veteran who sometimes spars with the White House on foreign policy, said the recent developments — including reports that the U.S. has stopped sharing intelligence with Kyiv — are benefiting an oligarchic adversary at the expense of a democratic ally.

If those policies don’t change, he warned, Ukraine’s defenders in the House — including some Republicans — will block the entirety of Trump’s post-midterm agenda.

“The Administration’s decision to reduce intel sharing to Ukraine & access to Starlink equates to aiding the invader & the war criminal who bombs cities,” Bacon wrote on the social platform X . “Does the Administration think it will get ANY support for the remainder of the 119th Congress? Their agenda is dead unless they change paths.”

Bacon is retiring at the end of this term. But his warning has teeth because he will still hold a seat in the lame-duck session, where Republican leaders are eyeing a number of proposals they want to push through before the year’s end. That list includes legislation to reauthorize farm and nutrition programs, extend federal surveillance powers, and fund the government to prevent a shutdown in mid-December.

It also includes a new round of Pentagon funding, which was expected before the elections but got pushed to the lame duck, at least in part to shield vulnerable Republicans from taking a tough vote related to the unpopular Iran war before voters went to the polls.

On Wednesday, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth sounded a bullish note on that package, including funds for drones, Trump’s “Golden Dome” project and new munitions stockpiles, which have dwindled as a result of the Iran conflict.

“We’re in lockstep with the White House,” Hegseth said. “Regardless of what happens in the midterms, we’re running fast — immediately — with the committees, to ensure that that reconciliation bill, at a minimum of $350 [billion], potentially more, ultimately fills up what this department needs.”

Bacon’s warning predicts that Trump will have a tougher time pushing that package through Congress, unless the administration changes its approach to the Russia-Ukraine war.

Trump has always had a relatively cozy relationship with Russian President Vladimir Putin going back to his first term, which marks a notable break from the adversarial association of past presidents in both parties.

Last year, Trump infuriated Ukraine’s allies when he and Vice President Vance confronted Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky at the White House and accused him of being insufficiently grateful for U.S. support in the war.

A similar anger resurfaced last week when Trump cut a deal with Putin that relaxed U.S. sanctions on Russian diesel fuel, providing Moscow with a boost in funding to help underwrite the war. It escalated again this week after reports that Trump had stopped sharing U.S. intelligence with Ukraine and cut off Kyiv’s access to a specialized satellite system empowering battlefield communications.

That satellite system is owned by SpaceX, one of Elon Musk’s companies, but funded by the Pentagon. Zelensky wasted no time going after Trump, warning that his decisions will help Putin kill more Ukrainians.

“It’s a pity that we are losing [a] strong partner,” Zelensky told Piers Morgan, a British journalist.

“It’s not about business for us, it’s just our lives,” he continued. “That’s why it’s painful when President Trump chooses one side — not our side. … We are OK that he’s in the middle. But if you’re in the middle you have to stay in the middle, not on the wrong side. “

“This is not the right side of history.”

articles.title: Trump scores win from liberal-leaning 9th Circuit in ICE enforcement showdown
articles.summary: The 9th Circuit ruled the Trump administration is "certain to succeed" against California's No Vigilantes Act, dealing a blow to Gavin Newsom.
articles.body: The Trump administration scored a victory at a liberal-leaning appeals court Wednesday, which temporarily blocked a section of a California law requiring plainclothes federal law enforcement agents to show their badges and identification when carrying out operations. The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals ruled the Trump administration was "certain to succeed" in its lawsuit against California, finding that the No Vigilantes Act’s identification requirement violates the Constitution’s supremacy clause, which says federal law takes priority when it conflicts with state law. "Section 10 explicitly overrides the federal government’s power to determine whether, how, and when to publicly identify its officers," the panel wrote. The preliminary injunction comes from a federal appeals court that has repeatedly clashed with the Trump administration over some of its signature immigration policies, including blocking efforts to withhold federal funding from sanctuary cities in 2018, restricting attempts to tighten asylum eligibility that same year and refusing to reinstate Trump's travel ban targeting several predominantly Muslim countries in 2017. FEDERAL COURT BLOCKS NEWSOM’S BID TO SHACKLE ICE IN TRUMP IMMIGRATION WIN The ruling comes as a major blow to California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom, widely viewed as a 2028 presidential hopeful. Newsom has positioned himself as a leading opponent of Trump's immigration agenda, signing a series of laws aimed at protecting immigrant communities, restricting federal immigration enforcement operations and increasing oversight of federal agents in the state. The Trump administration sued California over provisions in the No Vigilantes Act and No Secret Police Act, which restricts law enforcement officers from wearing face coverings, in November 2025. Judge Christina Snyder, a Clinton-appointed judge, initially blocked the No Secret Police Act's mask restriction for federal officers but declined to block the No Vigilantes Act's identification requirement. The Trump administration appealed Snyder's decision on the identification requirement, and the 9th Circuit temporarily blocked its enforcement in February before granting an injunction pending appeal in April. FEDERAL JUDGE BLOCKS NEW YORK LAW BANNING ICE AGENTS FROM WEARING MASKS California argued that its identification requirement did not amount to an unconstitutional regulation of the federal government because a state law crosses that line only when it "impose[s] substantial burdens on federal operations." But the appeals court ruled that the state never had the authority to directly regulate federal officials. "The burden of the regulation on federal operations, whether substantial or otherwise, is irrelevant," the court wrote. The liberal appeals court ruling drew praise from Trump administration officials, including Brett Shumate, assistant attorney general for the Justice Department's Civil Division. DOJ WARNS FORMER RED STATE IS BECOMING THE NEXT CALIFORNIA AS GOVERNOR EMBRACES ICE LIMITS "The Ninth Circuit agrees that California cannot regulate federal law enforcement," Schumate wrote on X. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "Today, the Ninth Circuit again affirms what common sense makes clear: California cannot regulate how Federal law enforcement officers carry out their jobs authorized by Congress," Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward, Jr. wrote on X. "Today's decision is a huge WIN for protecting the safety of our Nation's law enforcement officers and ensuring @POTUS 's promise to enforce our Nation's immigration laws." articles.title: Hochul dodges when pressed over victims of illegal immigrant crime: ‘Will you apologize?’
articles.summary: Bruce Blakeman pressed Kathy Hochul to apologize to families of victims killed by illegal immigrants, but the governor pivoted to ICE-related deaths.
articles.body: New York Gov. Kathy Hochul declined to directly apologize to the families of people killed by illegal immigrants after Republican challenger Bruce Blakeman confronted her over the issue during Tuesday night's gubernatorial debate. Hochul instead turned the exchange toward Americans killed by federal immigration agents. Looking directly at Hochul as he brought up several victims, Blakeman asked what she had to say to families who will "never get to sit at another Thanksgiving dinner, never be able to open their presents on their Christmas tree. "Will you apologize to them, and will you please return Sheridan Gorman's parents' calls to talk to you about your sanctuary policy?" he said. NEW YORK GOVERNOR DEBATE HEATS UP AS BLAKEMAN, HOCHUL SPAR OVER TRUMP, SANCTUARY STATUS, ICE SHOOTING Jose Medina-Medina, an illegal immigrant from Venezuela, faces charges related to the fatal shooting of Sheridan Gorman, an 18-year-old Loyola University Chicago student from Yorktown, New York, as she walked with friends near her campus late at night. Her death has fueled calls for change from her parents, who have taken aim at sanctuary policies that limit cooperation between local law enforcement and ICE. Hochul responded by calling all crimes "heartbreaking," adding, "I abhor all crimes, regardless of the perpetrator." She went on to say her administration has spent billions to "help law enforcement do their jobs" and reduce crime across the state. SHERIDAN GORMAN’S MOM SCORCHES DEM LAWMAKERS SHE SAYS REFUSED TO HEAR FAMILIES OF SLAIN AMERICANS "We have driven down crime to historic lows, especially violent crimes like shootings and murders, and that didn't come easy," she said. Instead, she brought up Renee Good and Alex Pretti, who were shot and killed during separate confrontations with federal immigration agents in Minneapolis in January. "When you're talking about ICE, what I find so shocking is that when an American mother was murdered by ICE agents, you said that her killing was justified," she fired back. I apologize for any pain that has happened to anyone." The exchange set off a wave of social media scrutiny, with critics accusing Hochul of not caring about the victims. "INSANE! Kathy Hochul can’t even apologize to victims of crimes committed by illegal aliens - or promise to return their calls," RNC Research posted on X. articles.title: Expert calls California 'Wild West' for surrogacy after couple charged with abusing surrogate-born children
articles.summary: Guojun Xuan and Silvia Zhang allegedly abused surrogate-born children while running an unlicensed California surrogacy agency from their home.
articles.body: The case of a California couple recently accused of abusing children born to surrogates exposes the pitfalls of an industry one expert described as the "wild west." Guojun Xuan, 66, and his wife, Silvia Zhang, 39, were arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit child abuse. Authorities said the couple operated their own surrogacy agency out of their home in Arcadia, California. "I say it all the time. It's the wild, Wild West," Kallie Fell, executive director of the Center for Bioethics and Culture, told Fox News Digital. SURROGATE WHO REFUSED ABORTION TAKES FIGHT TO SUPREME COURT AS BABY'S LIFE HANGS IN BALANCE Xuan and Zhang allegedly abused more than a dozen surrogate-born children — some as young as 2 months old — inside their multimillion-dollar Arcadia residence. Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman called the alleged abuse "appalling and revolting." OHIO MOM OF 16 CRADLES STOMACH IN COURT, PLEADS NOT GUILTY IN SEVERE ABUSE CASE INVOLVING OWN CHILDREN "This was not a home where these children were loved and nurtured," Hochman said when announcing the charges. "This was a home where these young children were systematically beaten and punished if they did not do what they were told." In addition to the alleged abuse, the couple operated Future Spring Surrogacy from their home, recruiting surrogates and paying them tens of thousands of dollars. At least eight surrogates reported aggressive tactics and false statements regarding the family's living situation, officials said. SURROGATE WHO REFUSED ABORTION ASKS SCOTUS TO INTERVENE AS BABY COULD BE MOVED OUT OF TEXAS "The thing about the case is that I wish it was shocking for me," said Fell, who opposes commercial surrogacy. "Because of the space I work in, I get to hear shocking stories around the globe — things that people don't realize the surrogacy industry has grown into. It's not just a place where couples who have been struggling with infertility go as a last resort to have a child." "I mean, this has really turned into, if you have enough money to pay for it, then you can, by any means necessary, really have a child in California," she added. SURROGATE, CALIFORNIA COUPLE CLASH IN COURT AS NEWBORN FIGHTS FOR LIFE AFTER HEART SURGERY Unlike in some states, a license is not required in California to open a surrogacy agency, and there is no comprehensive regulatory framework to oversee the industry across the state. Surrogacy is a billion-dollar global market used to help couples who are unable to conceive or carry a child. The issue, Fell noted, is that while the process is accessible to anyone who can afford it, there are no meaningful regulatory safeguards for the children born to surrogates. "I was a foster parent," she said. "My husband and I went through gobs of courses, gobs of home studies, background checks, everything — really under a microscope. The same is not true for surrogacy. It doesn't apply." As the surrogacy boom has expanded, foreign nationals — many from China — have increasingly used American surrogates to have children, according to a 2024 report by the Heritage Foundation. Because commercial surrogacy is completely illegal inside China, wealthy Chinese individuals and couples frequently look abroad, primarily to the U.S., to grow their families. While banned or heavily restricted in several other countries, cross-border surrogacy is not regulated at the federal level in the U.S., opening the door for foreign clients to secure American birthright citizenship for the resulting children, according to the conservative think tank. "Why do we need folks from overseas coming, renting wombs here in the United States?"

articles.title: Fox News Poll: Cost-of-living concerns weigh on GOP in midterms
articles.summary: A Fox News survey finds Trump's approval on inflation hitting a new low of 22% as six in 10 voters say cost of living is their top economic worry.
articles.body: When voters rate the economy and the president negatively just weeks before Election Day, the incumbent party is vulnerable, and that’s certainly the case in the latest Fox News survey. The economic landscape is stark. Six in 10 voters say the cost of living is their top economic worry, overshadowing government spending (15%), jobs and income inequality (7% each), tariffs (6%) and taxes (5%). Majorities rate the economy negatively (74%) and expect it to worsen next year (53%), while two-thirds are dissatisfied with how things are going in the country (66%). Few, 18%, say their family is better off compared to two years ago. Independents say they’re worse off (52%) and think the economy will get worse (70%). FOX NEWS POLL: IT’S A LONE STAR SENATE SHOWDOWN BETWEEN TALARICO AND PAXTON A majority of voters, 55%, say inflation is "not at all" under control. That’s up from a low of 45% earlier this year, and includes 30% of Republicans. President Donald Trump’s lowest job rating is on inflation: 22% approve, a new low. Last summer, 36% approved. Four years ago, before the 2022 midterms, 29% approved of former President Joe Biden’s performance on inflation. Disapproval of the job Trump is doing has reached 77% on inflation, 70% on the economy, 69% on tariffs and 64% on foreign policy. A smaller share, but still a majority, disapprove of his handling of immigration (56% disapprove), while border security is the only issue that is close to positive (50% approve, 50% disapprove). Trump’s overall job approval is 36%, his lowest ever in a Fox News survey for either term. It had been holding steady at 39% since May. The decline is mainly driven by decreases among voters under age 45, those with annual household income below $50,000, non-White voters, and those without a college degree. FOX NEWS POLL: MICHIGAN VOTERS SPLIT BETWEEN EL-SAYED AND ROGERS Approval stands at a low of 76% among Republicans. That’s down 3 points since last month, 12 points since September 2025, and 16 points since early in his second term (March 2025). As in most midterms, voters are prone to punish the party in power: 7 in 10 say they will vote to send a message to Trump, with nearly twice as many expressing opposition (47%) as support (25%). If the election were today, 54% of voters say they would back the Democratic candidate in their House district and 45% would support the Republican. That is outside the margin of error and is a wider lead than last month when Democrats were ahead by 51%-44%. The race narrows among those saying they are certain to vote, with the Democratic candidate ahead by 52%-46%. The survey finds about the same number self-identify as Democrats (43%) and Republicans (41%), and both parties feel equally certain about voting (62% and 64% respectively), while more Democrats (61%) than Republicans (52%) say they are extremely interested in the election. Party loyalty is solid: 98% of Democrats support their party’s candidate, and 94% of Republicans back theirs. Independents favor the Democrats by 26 points. The Democratic candidate is the choice among Whites with a degree, those under age 45, women, union households and Hispanics. The Republican is ahead among Whites without a college degree (White men without a degree in particular), those 65 and over, voters who attend religious services regularly, military veterans and White evangelical Christians. While 43% of Hispanic voters supported Trump in the 2024 election, just 31% prefer the Republican candidate this year. "When the country is this closely divided in terms of partisanship, slight differences in defection and turnout rates can make all the difference," said Republican pollster Daron Shaw, who helps conduct the Fox News Poll with Democrat Chris Anderson. "Republicans have time to close these apparent gaps, but it’s getting late." Meanwhile, Democrats lead on 10 out of 13 issue concerns. The top five voter concerns are government corruption (60% extremely concerned), inflation (58%), gas prices (50%), government leadership (49%), and healthcare (48%). And double digits more trust the Democrats than the Republicans to handle each of those. Republicans retain the advantage on crime (by 10 points) and border security (R+8), while views are closely divided on immigration (R+3). The Democrats are seen as better on healthcare (D+22), inflation (D+16), gas prices (D+12), voting rights (D+12), election integrity (D+12), government leadership (D+11), what’s taught in public schools (D+11), artificial intelligence (D+10), government corruption (D+10) and foreign policy (D+9). Republicans have lost ground on key issues compared to four years ago, when more voters trusted them by 21 points on border security, 13 points on inflation and 9 points on foreign policy. Other issues that voters are extremely concerned about are the Iran war (42%), immigration (35%), crime (34%), voter suppression (32%), AI technology (32%), what’s taught in public schools (29%), voter fraud (28%) and border security (25%). While corruption in government and inflation are the top two worries about both parties, far more Democrats (72% and 70%) than Republicans (47% and 49%) are extremely concerned. The issue that helps explain the Democrats’ advantage isn’t an issue at all. By a 14-point margin, more voters think the Democrats will do a better job "fighting for people like you." Majorities of White voters with a college degree (53%), men (52%), women (60%) and non-White voters (77%) think Democrats will fight for them. Whites without a college degree are split 49-49%. Despite their issue advantage, just 35% say Democrats have a clear plan for dealing with the country’s problems, and 33% say the same about the Republicans. That reverses the Republican advantage from July 2025, when 43% said the Republicans had a clear plan compared with 33% for the Democrats. There’s deep dissatisfaction with lawmakers: 15% approve of Congress, while 84% disapprove. Remarkably, that’s above the low of 9% approval in October 2013. Both parties are viewed negatively. The Democratic Party is underwater by 16 points (42% favorable, 58% unfavorable), while ratings of the GOP are net negative by 23 points (38% favorable, 61% unfavorable). Yet, favorable ratings fail to translate directly into vote choice. One third of those backing the Democratic candidate (31%) dislike the party, while 23% of those supporting the Republican dislike the GOP. Among the 26% who dislike both parties (double haters), Democrats lead 62%-36%. Here’s how polarized the parties are: Just 16% of Republicans say that Democrats love America and want what’s best for the U.S., and even fewer Democrats, 6%, think Republicans do. Compared to four years ago, the number of voters saying Democrats want what’s best for the country is up four points, while fewer say Republicans love the country now by 6 points. Poll-pourri Fifty-one percent of voters have a favorable view of capitalism compared with 32% for socialism. Compared to a year ago, positive ratings of capitalism are down 2 points while they are up 5 points for socialism. Eight in ten of those with a positive view of socialism support the Democratic candidate, while 6 in 10 of those viewing capitalism favorably back the Republican. Voters who plan to cast their ballots early favor the Democratic candidate (by 19 points) as do mail voters (D+33), while the candidate choice splits among those voting in person (early or on Election Day). Six in 10 oppose U.S. military action against Iran, and they back the Democrats by 56 points. CLICK HERE FOR CROSSTABS AND TOPLINE A new high of 46% think the U.S. is too supportive of Israel, and those voters favor the Democratic candidate by 42 points, while the 4 in 10 who think U.S. support of Israel is about right pick the Republican by 27 points. Nearly 6 in 10 have a negative view of artificial intelligence technology, and they back the Democratic candidate by 27 points. Conducted Oct. 9-12, 2026, under the direction of Beacon Research (D) and Shaw & Company Research (R), this Fox News survey includes interviews with a sample of 1,202 registered voters randomly selected from a national voter file. Respondents spoke with live interviewers on landlines (114) and cellphones (786) or completed the survey online after receiving a text (302). Results based on the full sample have a margin of sampling error of ±2.5 percentage points. Sampling error for results among subgroups is higher. In addition to sampling errors, question wording and order can influence results. Weights are generally applied to age, race, education and area variables to ensure the demographics are representative of the registered voter population. Sources for developing weight targets include the most recent American Community Survey, Fox News Voter Analysis and voter file data. Fox News’ Victoria Balara contributed to this report.

articles.title: How the House landscape is evolving: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. We’ve detailed in recent weeks how the Senate map has shifted in the final stretch of the midterm campaign. In today’s edition, Ben Kamisar digs into how the House landscape is changing. Plus, Andrea Mitchell examines the latest dilemma facing Ukraine. — Adam Wollner Republicans shift funds in the battle for the House By Ben Kamisar Facing a stormy political forecast, Republican groups are making hard choices about which candidates may get left out in the rain. Millions of dollars in GOP ad reservations have been cut in the last few days in a pair of battleground districts represented by Tom Kean Jr. of New Jersey and Mariannette Miller-Meeks of Iowa, according to AdImpact, an ad tracking service. Meanwhile, Republican groups are also pulling some resources from races in which they had hoped to put the pressure on Democratic lawmakers in competitive districts. Instead, they’ve been pouring money elsewhere, including in open seats or districts where Republican incumbents now appear locked in tougher contests. The GOP is still looking to press its big-money advantage across the House map. But more and more, it’s about playing defense in Republican-held seats — or even getting an extra boost in districts the party redrew ahead of the midterms — as places President Donald Trump won by around 10 percentage points in 2024 haven’t proved to be easy terrain. Kean had always faced tough re-election prospects in a seat Trump carried by just over 1 point two years ago. His district, in the New York City media market, is also one of the most expensive in the country for advertising. But Kean never fully regained his footing after a four-month disappearance from public view, which he later revealed was because he sought treatment for depression. Miller-Meeks is also no stranger to tough races, having won in 2020 by just six votes. But Iowa is looking unusually difficult for Republicans this year, as the state faced outsized impacts from tariffs and the Iran war. A source familiar with Republican outside groups’ spending strategy told NBC News that the money cut from Miller-Meeks’ district would be reallocated to Iowa’s 2nd and 3rd districts, where the GOP is also playing defense. Read more → Trump’s latest moves leave Ukraine on the defensive Analysis by Andrea Mitchell Facing midterm headwinds in usually reliably Republican farm states fueled in large part by the escalating cost of critical diesel oil, President Donald Trump shocked Ukraine and its European allies by lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports Friday. He proclaimed that would boost the global diesel supply, although energy experts said Russian refineries weren’t up to processing the fuel and Russia couldn’t export it all. Senators from both parties immediately objected that permitting Russian President Vladimir Putin to resume diesel exports would be illegal under 2022 congressionally mandated sanctions. It also violates recent legislation Trump had just signed into law as a memorial to the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C. Ukraine and its supporters were aghast that it would help Putin bail out his collapsing economy just as the European Union was about to announce increased economic pressure to get him to agree to a ceasefire. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy challenged Trump’s gift to Putin. In an outburst reminiscent of his infamous Oval Office harangue against Zelenskyy, Trump blamed him for a war that Putin had started and said he was now prolonging it, instead of acknowledging Putin’s refusal to negotiate. He also said Ukraine needs a new president. Significantly, Elon Musk, whose SpaceX Starlink satellite terminals are critical to Ukraine’s defense against Russian missiles and drones, said on X, “Zelenskyy has gone too far.” Multiple reports say U.S. negotiators warned Ukrainian officials at meetings in Miami on Friday that the U.S. could cut off intelligence, as well as the American weapons manufacturing supply line European allies had created for Ukraine. Suddenly Monday, Ukraine reported what officials called a “technical glitch” that was slowing down Starlink so its drones couldn’t combat five Russian ballistic missiles. Yesterday, there was another interruption — perhaps caused by bad weather, a Ukrainian official surmised to NBC News. Others were suggesting it was not likely to be a coincidence. Zelenskyy posted that Ukraine was hit by a major Russian attack and received no intelligence warning from its “partners.” Asked whether the U.S. had cut off intelligence, Trump said the U.S. was still sharing with Ukraine. But while he was in London today to brief British Prime Minister Andy Burnham on the growing crisis, Zelenskyy cited wave after wave of drones — 124 overnight Tuesday and 145 more during the day — with no warning from the U.S. or reliable satellite intelligence from Starlink. NBC News reported that Ukrainian officials say SpaceX has imposed new limitations on some Starlink services and has asked the U.S. for clarification. Retiring Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told Musk on X, “please tell me these overnight disruptions to Starlink terminals in Ukraine were unintended — that @SpaceX is doing everything it can to fix a temporary glitch. I’m confident this does not reflect a change in SpaceX policy because if so, intentionally degrading Ukraine’s ability to defend itself might be construed as aiding and abetting a mass murderer. Can you confirm that’s not SpaceX’s intent?” He went on to write: “Supporting Ukrainian sovereignty— or at the very least, allowing for it — should not be a gray area for the U.S. government or for American corporations.” Musk, the largest known single contributor to Republican midterm campaigns, also controls the critical satellite source in that and other war zones. The Pentagon has ultimate authority over how it is deployed. That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner. articles.title: DOJ threatens emergency legal action against California over suspected noncitizen voters
articles.summary: The Justice Department threatens emergency legal action against California over suspected noncitizens on voter rolls ahead of midterm elections.
articles.body: The Justice Department is threatening emergency legal action against California election officials unless they take steps to prevent suspected noncitizens from voting in November's midterm elections, setting a Thursday deadline as state officials push back. In letters sent Tuesday, Acting Deputy Attorney General R. Trent McCotter demanded that California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan review a list of potentially ineligible voters within 48 hours. The DOJ instructed officials to segregate ballots from individuals whose citizenship cannot be verified and warned it would seek emergency legal relief if its demands were not met by noon Eastern on Oct. 15. A DOJ spokesperson told Fox News Digital that thousands of potential foreign nationals ineligible to vote have been identified on California's voter rolls statewide, not just in Los Angeles County. MAP IT: DOJ ILLEGAL VOTING CRACKDOWN SWEEPS 17 STATES AS RAZOR-THIN ELECTIONS FACE SCRUTINY "This should not be controversial, as the criminal statute is clear: only American citizens may vote in federal elections. It is a federal crime for noncitizens to vote in U.S. elections, and the DOJ is asking California to ensure that is not occurring," the spokesperson said. California Attorney General Rob Bonta, a Democrat, pushed back during a Wednesday news conference, accusing the Trump administration of attempting to intimidate voters and promoting false allegations of widespread voter fraud. JUSTICE DEPARTMENT CHARGES 16 ACROSS MULTIPLE STATES WITH ALLEGED ILLEGAL VOTING, ELECTION CRIMES "There is no widespread voter preference, voter fraud problem. It doesn't exist. It is a lie. It is a conspiracy theory," Bonta said. Bonta said his office is working with the secretary of state and Los Angeles County officials to review their options. STATE DEPARTMENT CONSIDERS SHARING PASSPORT RECORDS FOR VOTER CITIZENSHIP CHECKS Meanwhile, Logan said his office received a password-protected USB drive purportedly containing voter records but has not accessed it because of cybersecurity concerns. "We have not accessed the drive because doing so would conflict with established data privacy and information security protocols. We do not consider the device a secure medium. Additionally, the letter does not specify the number of individuals involved or describe the information contained in the records," he said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The dispute comes as Californians are already casting ballots ahead of the Nov. 3 election. Federal law prohibits noncitizens from voting in federal elections, though the DOJ has not established that the individuals identified have cast illegal ballots.

articles.title: Watchdog group sues Trump administration over Jared Kushner’s government work
articles.summary: A watchdog group filed suit Wednesday alleging President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner’s current role as a top envoy for the administration is unlawful and raises numerous conflict-of-interest concerns.
articles.body: A watchdog group filed suit Wednesday alleging President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner’s current role as a top envoy for the administration is unlawful and raises numerous conflict-of-interest concerns. Kushner is wielding tremendous influence internationally “without having been confirmed by the Senate and without having filed a single financial disclosure,” the suit by Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, or CREW, reads. Kushner “has not been properly vetted for his government role, and he has evaded transparency obligations that aim to ensure he exercises government authority for the good of the American people and not himself,” the suit reads. The suit seeks to have Kushner removed from his position or at least file financial disclosure statements. Chad Mizelle, an attorney for Jared Kushner, said in a statement that the suit “is without merit.” “Both outside ethics counsel and government ethics attorneys have reviewed Jared Kushner’s volunteer government service and confirmed that his arrangements comply with applicable ethics requirements. Jared receives no government salary or compensation, pays his own expenses, and will continue working with counsel to ensure ongoing compliance,” Mizelle said. A White House spokesperson ripped CREW and the suit in a separate statement. “CREW is an unserious, Trump-deranged organization that has been attacking President Trump, his family, and his administration since the first term. Jared Kushner is a proven dealmaker” with a record of success “that more than speaks for itself,” the spokesperson, Anna Kelly, said in a statement. “His personal business activities have nothing to do with his diplomatic engagements, which he conducts on a volunteer basis at the President’s request and while paying his own expenses,” the statement said. The suit mentions numerous overlapping interests in Kushner’s diplomatic and business work. “He represents the United States in the highest profile global conflicts, including the country’s efforts to end wars between Israel and Hamas, Ukraine and Russia, and the United States and Iran. He negotiates directly with foreign leaders,” the group’s filing says. “Simultaneously, Kushner is also a private businessman. He runs an investment firm with over $6 billion in assets under management. Approximately 99% of those assets are owned by foreign investors, including the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and the United Arab Emirates. The firm holds significant investments abroad, including in Israel,” the suit says, all of which “present a heightened risk of financial conflicts of interest.” It adds that “declining a salary and formal title does not change the reality of Kushner’s role — he exercises significant executive authority and has done so continuously throughout most of President Trump’s second term. And it certainly does not free him from the constitutional constraints of the Appointments Clause or the obligation to file public financial disclosures under the Ethics Act.” The suit seeks to bar Kushner from occupying his government position without Senate confirmation. It says that, if he’s a private citizen, “his exercise of government power would violate the private non-delegation doctrine, which prohibits the delegation of government power to private entities.” Despite the scope of Kushner’s duties, a White House official said there’s nothing unusual about the use of a private envoy. “The use of private diplomatic envoys to deal with delicate international situations is a presidential practice that dates back to George Washington’s presidency,” the official said.

articles.title: Lawyers for N.Y. man shot by ICE say officer fired into car without warning
articles.summary: Lawyers for a man wounded by an immigration officer while driving with his young son in New York said in a court filing Wednesday that the agent who shot him never identified himself before he ran up to the car, smashed one of its windows, then fired several shots into the vehicle.
articles.body: NEW YORK — Lawyers for a man wounded by an immigration officer while driving with his young son in New York said in a court filing Wednesday that the agent who shot him never identified himself before he ran up to the car, smashed one of its windows, then fired several shots into the vehicle. The account by lawyers for Oscar Belgal contrasted sharply with the version of events outlined by Department of Homeland Security officials. They have said officers opened fire only after Belgal smashed his car into two government vehicles and “accelerated toward other officers.” The Legal Aid Society, in a petition filed in Brooklyn federal court seeking Belgal's release, said he had picked up his son from school on Oct. 8 and was stopped in front of a fire hydrant, looking for a parking spot, when “an anonymous, masked man” stormed up to the vehicle with his gun drawn, followed by other masked men with guns. “The men did not identify themselves, show any documents or otherwise communicate with Oscar in any substantive way," Belgal's lawyers wrote. "Instead, without identifying himself, the first man struck and shattered Oscar’s window and began firing a pistol into Oscar’s car while his son cowered in the back seat. One of those bullets struck Oscar in the neck and he immediately began to bleed.” New York City police security camera footage released by the department last week shows some of the encounter but doesn't conclusively resolve the dispute about how the shooting happened. The video shows a man wearing a sweatshirt and a red hat running up to the car with his gun pointed at Belgal, then immediately using the barrel of his gun to bash the driver’s side window. The window shatters on the second blow. A second officer comes into view alongside the car and draws his gun. Belgal then pulls into the street, away from the two officers. The car pulls out of view of the camera, with the officer in the red hat in pursuit. Whatever happened next didn't appear on the NYPD's security cameras, but the chase ended just a moment later, with Belgal's damaged car resting against a concrete barrier with bullet holes in its windshield and a rear window. Video from bystanders and NYPD body camera footage show that ICE officers handcuffed Belgal and tended to a gunshot wound to his neck as he sat on the pavement outside the car. NYPD officers took Belgal to a nearby hospital. DHS didn't comment Wednesday on the claims by Belgal's lawyers, saying the incident remains under investigation. But DHS officials have maintained that ICE officers fired their weapons because they believed their lives were in danger. Belgal’s lawyers said he didn’t learn the men were ICE officers until he awoke later in the hospital. They say he remains detained at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, where he has yet to receive surgery to remove the bullet lodged in his neck. They also say he has lost sensation on the left side of his face and is suffering from impaired hearing. The Federal Bureau of Prisons, which manages the jail, didn’t immediately comment. “Mr. Belgal’s detention was unlawful from its inception. ICE officers shot him in the neck in front of his five year-old son, failed to provide him with immediate medical assistance, and now continue to hold him in a facility notorious for medical neglect,” said Perry McAninch and Elyssa Williams, the lawyers representing Belgal. At a news conference last week, Marcos Charles, the head of ICE's enforcement and removal operations, said Belgal refused orders to exit his vehicle and then accelerated and smashed into two government vehicles as ICE officers tried to block him from driving away. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has maintained officers didn’t know a child was in the car and blamed Belgal for putting his son's life in danger.

articles.title: ICE pushes back on report suggesting body cameras that automatically record
articles.summary: The immigration agency rejects a report from a government watchdog recommending improvements to its body camera policy.
articles.body:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), a United States agency that has taken a central role in President Donald Trump’s mass deportation campaign, has rejected a government report calling for its agents to wear body cameras that automatically activate.

On Wednesday, the Government Accountability Office, a nonpartisan agency that provides research to Congress, released a report recommending an update to ICE guidelines for camera usage.

It suggested that “automated camera activation” would be helpful in situations where “unexpected and unplanned incidents, unrelated to sensitive operations, result in use of force by or against personnel”.

“Given the important role of body-worn cameras in law enforcement activities, we maintain that additional controls are needed to help ensure that ICE personnel capture footage in accordance with policy,” the report said.

Automatic activation, it added, would address difficulties ICE agents face in manually turning on their cameras during enforcement operations.

But ICE has rejected the recommendation for automatic activation, which could be triggered by an agent pulling a gun or turning on a car siren. The agency cited privacy concerns.

But the Trump administration faces public pressure to improve transparency during its immigration raids.

Agents from ICE and other agencies such as Customs and Border Protection (CBP) have faced accusations of excessive force and civil liberties violations.

In January, two US citizens – Renee Good and Alex Pretti – were shot to death in separate shootings in Minneapolis, Minnesota, during immigration operations.

The New York Times estimated in July that immigration agents had opened fire on at least 25 people since the start of Trump’s second term. A CBS News review updated this week counts at least 30 shootings, with nine people killed and 13 others wounded.

ICE has often blamed such incidents on aggression against its agents, and it has argued that its officers have opened fire to defend themselves from danger.

But in several cases, that rationale has come under scrutiny.

Critics argued that video footage in Good’s fatal shooting disproved government statements alleging that she had weaponised her vehicle against agents. Her car, according to observers, appeared to be turning away from agents, not towards them.

In another case, ICE agent Christian Castro was accused of making false statements about a shooting that resulted in injury to Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis, a Venezuelan man living in Minneapolis.

Castro faces federal charges for allegedly lying about being attacked with a snow shovel and broom before the shooting, after video footage contradicted his account. Castro pleaded not guilty last month.

More recently, on October 8, immigration agents shot a man named Oscar Belgal in New York City while his five-year-old son was in the backseat of his car. ICE stated that Belgal appeared to be “going towards officers” in his car when they opened fire.

On Tuesday, a judge rejected the government’s effort to have Belgal deported.

Activists say better recording procedures for body camera footage could help clarify what happened in such incidents.

But the Trump administration has largely refused to implement reforms to ICE protocol.

Earlier this year, Democrats in Congress delayed funding for the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, on the basis that significant changes needed to be made to reduce incidents of excessive force.

The department said on Wednesday that automatically recording cameras could result in “the unauthorised recording of sensitive interactions with informants or victims”.

The agency added that all ICE offices had received body cameras as of August 5, but that training in their use was still ongoing and would be finished “soon”.
