articles.title: How data centres became the sleeper issue that could decide the US midterms
articles.summary: Democrats and Republicans alike are coming out against data centre development, amid growing backlash across the US.
articles.body:
A year ago, a longtime US senator was not thinking much about data centres. ​​

Now, according to one of his advisers, he is having regular meetings with staff to track their impact and working on new legislation aimed at curbing their rapid expansion across the country.

"This happens sometimes, something starts slow and then it goes fast", the senior policy adviser to the Democratic senator told the BBC. The person spoke on condition of anonymity as they are not permitted to speak to the press.

The 180-degree turn in this senator's attention was driven almost entirely by a growing wave of public backlash that has seen politicians across the country scramble to keep up. Public sentiment has turned against the expansion of data centres, the large warehouses that store processing power needed for internet activity.

Packed with rows and rows of computer chips, sometimes seven-feet high, data centres have turned into more than infrastructure for the internet. They are now the physical embodiment of the recent and explosive growth of artificial intelligence (AI) technology, and the varied fears people associate with it.

"I don't want to be the guinea pig for this," Indiana resident Angelita Soriano told the BBC.

A new Amazon data centre is being built directly across the street from her home. When complete, the 26-building structure will take up more than a square mile in her neighbourhood and maintain 782 diesel-powered generators.

Some data centres are even larger. In Ohio, a joint effort between OpenAI, Nvidia, SB Energy and the US Department of Energy is set to build a data centre complex that will stretch for roughly six square miles, the same size as most townships in the US.

There are about 3,000 data centres currently operating in the US, with that number potentially doubling in the next few years, according to a report by Pew Research Center.

Data centres are built through very local rules and permits, meaning federal lawmakers like US senators have little say in the process.

Yet, opposition has become so strong so quickly in the US that suddenly, politicians at all levels are now all but required to take a stand.

"This isn't just an issue on the left, there is huge pushback among conservatives to data centres," Chloe Autio, an AI policy adviser, said. "Whoever articulates a clear position and sticks to it, in either party, really stands to benefit."

Her analysis was echoed by the adviser to the US Senator working on data centre legislation.

"There is a clear policy need here that we're looking to fill," he said. "This is a major backlash across the country - constituents are seeing the impacts of data centres and they do not like them."

That has put many on Capitol Hill - even Republicans - in direct conflict with President Donald Trump, who has championed the unrestrained growth of AI technology.

Trump has dubbed the backlash to data centres a "sick conspiracy" and said people and towns working to keep the buildings out are "backwards and poor".

His ire has been used as a boon to Democratic politicians looking to draw midterm votes from unhappy or undecided constituents.

The BBC spoke to residents of Indiana, Arizona, Michigan, Pennsylvania and Oregon, all of whom have been organising locally against the development of data centres. They expressed concerns about many aspects of the buildings, including their size, construction and operational noise, their impact on air, water and energy resources, as well as the speed at which they seem to be approved by local authorities.

During the first few months of this year, community groups organising against data centres more than doubled to 833, cropping up in almost every US state, according to research from Data Center Watch. The firm collects data for AI industry stakeholders and is part of an AI startup 10a Labs.

Stephanie Maldonado, the political director of LUCHA, a community organising group based in Arizona, referred to the push back against data centres as "a David and Goliath story" that began several years ago.

"People have been ready to put a stop to it," Maldonado added. "Now, people are angry."

New national polling shows that AI regulation and data centres are among some of the top issues for voters this election cycle, behind the ongoing Iran War and various aspects of the economy.

Proponents of building data centres often argue the projects will create more, and better paying, local jobs.

Yet, recent research from Brookings Institution, a non-partisan policy research group, found that a new data centre creates between 100 and 200 local jobs, which is "fewer than industry advocates claim". The projects also have essentially no impact on local wages.

Arizona Governor Katie Hobbs was one such proponent - until public pressure pushed her to the other side of the issue. In July, she enacted a three-year pause on any new tax break given to a company for a data centres project.

Arizona is far from the only state to see politicians react to data centre backlash.

Abdul El Sayed, a Democrat running for Senate in Michigan, made new rules and regulations for data centres a clear part of his successful primary campaign for Senate.

In the race for governor of Georgia, a Democrat who is calling for a pause on data centre development is in a dead heat with a Republican who disagrees.

Republican Senator John Husted of Ohio, who is fighting to keep his seat against Democrat Sherrod Brown, has also had to shift his position. Recent polls have found that the majority of Ohio voters oppose data centres. He has softened his support, saying that their arrival should be up to local citizens and elected officials.

Meanwhile, Brown has stumped on his opposition to new data centres. He leads Husted in recent polls.

Husted's trouble in Ohio led the National Republican Senatorial Committee, the major fundraising arm for conservatives in the Senate, to write in a private memo that Republican politicians needed to entirely reframe how they spoke to voters on data centres.

"This has become a sleeper issue for the entire election cycle", the NRSC added.

Texas is perhaps the most clear cut example of how backlash has turned into an undeniable issue for even the most pro-business politician.

The state currently has almost 300 operational data centres, with another 170 planned for development, according to Pew data.

At the end of last year, Republican Governor Greg Abbott had boasted of Texas as "the epicentre of AI development" because of the number of data centres it housed.

Within months he was backtracking, citing concerns of "safety and quality of life".

It could play a part in the state's upcoming senate race too.

Democrat James Talarico's campaign is pushing for an end to "sweetheart tax deals" for Big Tech. He's now seen as a frontrunner for the historically Republican seat, where he is facing off against Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton.

Paxton said in a late September interview that there was still "plenty of open space in Texas that we can put data centres".

Many of the actions or proposals that have come from politicians looking to appease or address these voters are temporary. Most of the moratoriums, for instance, will end in one to three years.

It is possible that the political winds will have shifted by the time such moratoriums expire, leaving Big Tech and AI firms to build as they wish.

For now, people's feelings toward them are strong.

Balaji Tammabattula, the chief executive of Barupon, is developing a roughly 700-acre data centre and technology campus in Liberty, Texas. Despite the buildings being designed to use rain capture for water and supply its own energy needs, an increasingly common design for major data centre projects, Tammabattula told the BBC that people in the community oppose the project out of hand.

"There's just such a high level of tension from the jump that you can't really even break through with the facts," he said.

During a recent community event, Tammabattula said he tried to speak one-on-one with a woman who was vociferously opposed to the project.

"She just looked right at me and said, 'Get the hell out of my state.'"

articles.title: Trump announces Taiwan’s plans to buy US gas
articles.summary: {beacon} Energy & Environment Energy & Environment The Big Story Trump announces Taiwan’s plans to buy US gas President Trump announced Tuesday that Taiwan has agreed to purchase 30 percent of gas from the Alaska pipeline over the next 20 years. © Photo Credit: AP Photo/Alex Brandon Speaking at a campaign rally in Wasilla,…
articles.body:
Trump announces Taiwan’s plans to buy US gas

President Trump announced Tuesday that Taiwan has agreed to purchase 30 percent of gas from the Alaska pipeline over the next 20 years.

Speaking at a campaign rally in Wasilla, Alaska, Trump said Taiwan will invest $4.4 billion into the project on top of $50 billion already committed by South Korea.

The president was quick to credit incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska), who is facing a competitive election bid, with the announcement.

“I have to say that Dan Sullivan helped me get this done. Thank you, Dan,” Trump said at the event.

Earlier this month, Trump announced South Korea would invest up to $200 billion into U.S. energy infrastructure, including toward a natural gas pipeline in Alaska. The investment also sought to fund a natural gas plant in Texas and eight new nuclear power plants across the U.S.

South Korean officials apparently disputed some of the specifics of the president’s earlier announcement.

Welcome to The Hill’s Energy & Environment newsletter, I’m Rachel Frazin — keeping you up to speed on the policies impacting everything from oil and gas to new supply chains.

Did someone forward you this newsletter? Subscribe here.

How policy will affect the energy and environment sectors now and in the future:

President Trump issued pardons at a campaign rally in Alaska on Tuesday for two diesel mechanics who were previously charged with and plead guilty to violating the Clean Air Act.

A federal judge on Tuesday ordered the Trump administration to stop work on East Potomac Park, the site of East Potomac Golf Links and a property the president has been eyeing for redevelopment.

President Trump announced early Wednesday that “massive” oil, gas and mineral exploration is “getting ready to begin” in Greenland.

EPA administrator Lee Zeldin had a wide-ranging press gaggle on Wednesday. Here are a couple key things he said:

Zeldin said that he was “days, not weeks” away from signing a proposed rule that’s expected to relax methane restrictions for oil and gas production.

The administrator said reforms to the Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA) could be part of Congress’s lame duck session. “We provide technical assistance with ideas on ways to do TSCA reform. This is something that is a subject of bipartisan conversation,” he said. “It’s a topic that could be part of the lame duck session.”

Asked whether proposed waivers that could allow water utilities more time before they have to filter out toxic forever chemicals were meant to be common or rare, Zeldin did not directly say, but he said there have been significant advancements in affordable technology in recent months. “”My confidence level today is a lot higher than it was a year ago that water systems are going to be able to treat for PFAS at far less cost,” he said.

articles.title: White House punches back at Chicago Mayor Johnson over reparations demands
articles.summary: Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson alleged Trump enriched the ultra-rich while ignoring descendants of the formerly enslaved, drawing a White House rebuke.
articles.body: The White House punched back at Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson Wednesday after the progressive mayor claimed President Donald Trump neglected compensation for descendants of formerly enslaved Black Americans while favoring the wealthy. Johnson appeared on the "Native Land Pod" podcast Sunday to discuss his administration's crime reduction efforts in Chicago, where violent crime rates have fallen sharply, according to the Johnson administration and Chicago Police Department data. Speaking with hosts Angela Rye, Bakari Sellers and Andrew Gillum, Johnson argued that public safety "has to be something more than just policing," highlighting city investments in "mental behavioral healthcare, promoting detectives and expanding and investing in CVI (community violence intervention)." REPARATIONS ACTIVISTS CALL OUT BLUE STATES FOR USING SLAVERY HISTORY TO FUND BROADER AGENDA The podcast hosts turned to a recent Truth Social post by Trump targeting Illinois leadership over crime. "Chicago is suffering an unprecedented and particularly violent crime wave that is getting worse by the day," Trump posted on Oct. 6. "The Federal Government can extinguish it quickly and completely, but the Mayor of Chicago, or the Governor of Illinois, must ask for our help. What is wrong with them? Why aren’t they asking? TIME IS OF THE ESSENCE! President DJT." Johnson pushed back against the president’s statement, alleging Trump enriched wealthy Americans while ignoring the demands of "descendants of the formerly enslaved." "He's so sorry. It's real pathetic, right, because it's so disingenuous. … This is the president who just released the largest upward transfer of wealth into the hands of the ultrarich at the expense of the demands of those of us who are descendants of the formerly enslaved," Johnson said. "The largest upward transfer of wealth at the expense of education, housing, health care, transportation, good-paying jobs, which literally were all the demands of the formerly enslaved." TRUMP ADMIN VOWS TO STOP REPARATIONS PROGRAMS, ACCUSES OFFICIALS OF 'VIRTUE SIGNALING' TO GET 'VOTES' Johnson also said Trump "cut [the] violence prevention budget by $800 million," slamming the president for being concerned "about the wrong borders" as illegal weapons pour into Chicago. "He cut the ATF budget by 30%. My local police department has worked in tandem with the AFT to get illegal weapons off the streets of Chicago. This year alone, we have removed almost 9,000 illegal weapons off the street." The White House dismissed Johnson's claims and called on the mayor to focus on local public safety. "Government programs that dole out money based on race are illegal," a White House spokesperson told Fox News Digital Wednesday. "Chicago would be better served if Mayor Johnson focused more on lowering his city’s homicide rate instead of advocating for divisive, unconstitutional government action." BLACK CHICAGOANS CALL ON REPARATIONS FROM GOVERNMENT, MONEY DEPOSITS LIKE 'STIMULUS' CHECKS According to the mayor's office, Chicago has seen notable drops in violent crime since Johnson took office in May 2023, including double-digit decreases in homicides, shootings and overall violent crime. Chicago has "achieved historic double-digit decreases in crime and violence" in 2025, a spokesperson for Johnson told Fox News Digital, and is on track to see even further decreases in violent crime in 2026, with homicides down 3.8%, shootings down 1.3%and robberies down 20.9% from the same period last year. While Johnson did not explicitly use the word "reparations" during the interview, a spokesperson pointed Fox News Digital to the city’s reparations initiatives. Johnson previously signed an executive order establishing a 40-member reparations task force intended to address "historical harms committed against Black Chicagoans and their ancestors." In March, Johnson announced the Repair Chicago public engagement initiative aimed at gathering lived experiences from Black residents to inform future municipal policy and direct equity measures. The push for reparations in the region comes as the federal government ramps up legal scrutiny of local programs. Nearby Evanston, Illinois, launched a first-of-its-kind reparations program in 2021, offering $25,000 grants to eligible Black residents or their direct descendants for housing and home repairs, funded by local taxes on legal recreational marijuana sales. To date, Evanston has distributed more than $7 million of an allotted $20 million fund. Earlier this year, the city's Reparations Committee cleared an additional wave of funding for 44 residents. However, the Trump administration’s Department of Justice (DOJ) has signaled plans to challenge race-conscious distribution models. Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division previously told Fox News Digital that local officials pushing these measures are "virtue signaling" to win votes. CHICAGO REPARATIONS ADVOCATES SAY FEDERAL GOV MORALLY OWES '7 QUADRILLION DOLLARS' IN SLAVE LABOR Federal intervention is expanding elsewhere as well. articles.body:
Democrat Cait Conley told Rep. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.) during a televised debate Wednesday night not to “mansplain” to her about domestic abuse as the pair discussed an alleged gang rape at a Cornell University fraternity in 2024.

During the debate, the moderator from PIX11 News—an affiliate of Nexstar Media Group, which also owns The Hill— asked Conley and Lawler whether there should be a federal definition or law for consent, after the Cornell rape allegations drew national headlines .

Conley had accused Lawler of failing to call out Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio), who is under intense scrutiny after allegations leveled by his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, that he hurled hot water at her, pointed a gun at her head and broke their daughter’s collarbone.

“First of all, I did not blame Emily. I know both of them. It’s very tragic, and it should be dealt with in family court,” Lawler said, before firing back at Conley for taking “money from Eliot Spitzer, who trafficked young women across state lines for the purpose of sexually abusing them, and you refuse to return those funds. You refuse to denounce him in any way.”

Spitzer held a fundraiser for Conley last year, according to Politico, which Conley has faced intense criticism for. Spitzer stepped down as New York governor in 2008 after a prostitution scandal.

Conley then replied, “I do not need you to mansplain to me what domestic abuse and sexual assault against women is and the appropriate response. Don’t start. Sit over there. I do not need you to mansplain to me, Mike.”

The moderator had also asked both candidates whether they agree with the Education Department’s decision to formally rescind the Biden-era Title IX interpretation that gave sex-based discrimination protections to students on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity. Both Lawler and Conley said they opposed the change.

The two also clashed over the war in Iran, with Conley arguing that she does believe “that we need to take military action to ensure that Iran does not obtain a nuclear weapon.”

Differing from most Democrats, she said initially, “I did agree with the strikes that the administration took on the targeted locations associated with the nuclear weapons development programs in Iran, and I believe that is the smart approach that we should have continued to sustain in order to degrade their capabilities.”

However, Conley argued the Trump administration got “us into this war of choice in a way that is not making America any less or any more safe. I think this is a real challenge that Congress should be stepping up to the plate on.”

She said Lawler has “just continued to give Donald Trump a green light with zero accountability,’ instead of holding the president and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth accountable.

Asked why he thinks it is necessary for America to remain in this conflict with Iran, Lawler said, “Because I’m not going to put politics above a righteous decision about our national security. Iran cannot possess a nuclear weapon. Period.”

“That is why I have voted against efforts to undermine our national security,” Lawler said.

The pair also went head to head over artificial intelligence, data centers, military aid to Israel and other topics. A recent Emerson College and PIX11 survey found Lawler trailing behind Conley by two percentage points.

The survey found around 48 percent of likely voters in the district supported Conley, while 46 percent backed the Republican lawmaker. The remaining respondents were still undecided less than five weeks out from the November election.

articles.title: Talarico debates Texas voters in CNN-Jubilee town hall amid tight Senate race
articles.summary: Texas Democrat James Talarico on Wednesday took questions from voters in a town hall hosted by CNN and Jubilee, appearing on stage solo as he calls for rival Republican Ken Paxton to debate in their closely watched Senate race. Talarico, a state lawmaker and Presbyterian seminarian, argued “we’re all on the same team” and called…
articles.body:
Texas Democrat James Talarico on Wednesday took questions from voters in a town hall hosted by CNN and Jubilee, appearing on stage solo as he calls for rival Republican Ken Paxton to debate in their closely watched Senate race.

Talarico, a state lawmaker and Presbyterian seminarian, argued “we’re all on the same team” and called for politicians of all stripes to “work together” to tackle issues including security at the state’s southern border, the rapid build-out of data centers and pocketbook pressures on Texans.

He also promised to “stand up to my own party” as he fielded questions about his faith, abortion and controversial past remarks. He also tackled conspiracy theories that surrounded his recent absence from the campaign trail due to the flu, railing against a “rage economy” in political discourse.

CNN’s Erin Burnett noted that the outlet offered Paxton the opportunity to appear, and that the invitation still stands. Paxton has avoided Talarico’s calls for a debate , though President Trump encouraged the Texas attorney general to do so.

“You may have noticed that I haven’t talked about my opponent at all tonight because I don’t want people to vote … just against Ken Paxton. I want them to vote for me,” Talarico said at the end of the 90-minute program. “But the last thing I will say is that we are running against the most corrupt politician in Texas.”

Talarico is ahead of Paxton by roughly 2.5 percentage points in the latest polling average from Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Though Republicans have dominated statewide offices in Texas for decades, this year’s Senate race is rated a toss-up as Talarico fuels hope of a rare flip.

“I think the responsible thing to do when you have something like the flu is to stay at home and not get other people sick,” Talarico told Burnett, when asked about Republican-driven rumors about his recent absence from the campaign trail.

“I mean, that decision to stay home for a week sent my opponent and his conspiracy theorists spiraling. I opened up social media and learned that I apparently had dropped out of the race, had flown to a mental hospital in Ohio, that I had died. This is crazy,” he said.

The Democrat also pushed back against interpretations of some of his past remarks, including a 2020 comment calling capitalism an “oppressive system” in contrast with his current “proud capitalist” stance.

“I was talking about the system we have now, which is actually not capitalism; it’s crony capitalism,” he said.

He also defended his 2021 comments that “God is nonbinary,” which Republicans have seized as an attack line.

“When I said that, I was being provocative,” Talarico said. “But I think what I was saying is actually not controversial theologically. The idea that we can’t define God using human categories-not only did I say that, but the late Charlie Kirk said that, the late Pope Benedict said that.”

Faith was a major topic of the night, with Talarico telling voters that “the cross is the shape of reality … at the center of our shared faith.”

Asked by an independent Texan about his pro-choice stance in the context of his faith, Talarico stressed that voters can find “common ground” on policy solutions even if they come to “different moral and ethical conclusions” about the legality of abortion.

“What I think we can do is actually come together on reducing the number of unplanned pregnancies and the number of abortions, because if we treat this issue as a public health problem and not a culture war problem, then we can actually make progress together,” Talarico said.

And as he runs a blue campaign in deep red Texas, Talarico also stressed that he would buck his party in order to put Lone Star State constituents ahead of Washington interests and say things “a lot of Democrats aren’t willing to say.”

“I am not running for the U.S. Senate to represent New York or California. I’m not running for the U.S. Senate to represent the Democratic Party. I am running for Senate to represent all 31 million Texans, and I will, I will, I will always do what’s best for Texas, even if that means standing up to my own party.”

Republicans have the home field advantage in Texas, which went to Trump in each of his three presidential cycles and where Democrats haven’t won statewide in decades. But this year’s race is considered one of the cycle’s most competitive in the country, putting the GOP on defense in the red stronghold.

Three new polls released this week in Texas show Talarico leading Paxton, who won the GOP Senate nod in Texas over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn, in the battleground race. The energy around the campaign has drawn comparisons to Beto O’Rourke’s 2018 bid, when the Democrat came within just a few points of toppling Sen. Ted Cruz (R).

In what some saw as a sign of the high stakes, Republicans held their first-ever midterm convention last month in Dallas, putting a spotlight on Paxton — though the New York Times recently leaked an audio clip in which the Republican Senate hopeful said the convention “dropped our numbers.”

Trump has since made two more visits to the state to stump for Paxton, and Vice President Vance rallied there last week. Trump has also said last week that Talarico “should immediately report to a Debate Stage” to face off with Paxton.

Republicans’ Senate campaign arm swiftly responded to the Wednesday night town hall.

“James Talarico can tell all the tall tales he wants, but Texans won’t believe him,” said NRSC regional press secretary Samantha Cantrell in a statement.

articles.title: Trump’s approval rating hits record low in Fox News poll
articles.summary: President Trump’s overall approval rating hit a record low for either of his terms, according to a new Fox News survey amid growing voter dissatisfaction with his handling of key issues. The Fox News poll found 36 percent of respondents approved of Trump’s overall handling of the presidency, while 64 percent disapproved. The decline, Fox…
articles.body:
President Trump’s overall approval rating hit a record low for either of his terms, according to a new Fox News survey amid growing voter dissatisfaction with his handling of key issues.

The Fox News poll found 36 percent of respondents approved of Trump’s overall handling of the presidency, while 64 percent disapproved.

The decline, Fox News noted, was most notable among likely voters aged 45 and under, people with an annual household income below $50,000, non-White voters and people without a college degree.

Among Republican respondents, 76 percent approved of Trump and 23 percent disapproved, whereas 98 of Democratic respondents disapproved of Trump and 2 percent approved. Meanwhile, 78 percent of independent respondents disapproved of Trump and 22 percent approved.

The poll also reported only 22 percent approved of Trump’s handling of inflation, compared to 36 percent reported in a survey from last summer.

Disapproval of the president on other issues included 70 percent disapproval of his handling of the economy, 69 percent on tariff-related issues, 64 percent on foreign policy and 56 percent on immigration.

Trump’s handling of border security was rated highest among key issues, as 50 percent approved and 50 percent disapproved.

The president’s reelection campaign in 2024 focused on lowering prices for voters. However, the war with Iran has resulted in oil price spikes that have translated to higher energy costs nationwide.

Regular gas in the U.S. costs about $4.33 per gallon as of Wednesday, $1.25 higher than a year ago, according to data from AAA .

Trump initially predicted the war would last for a few weeks but has struggled to find an off-ramp despite blows to his approval rating and the GOP. He recently stated the conflict would end following the 2026 midterm elections but did not provide details on how that will happen.

The president acknowledged “ it’s possible ” the Iran war could cost him the November elections. However, he has also brushed aside concern about rising costs, saying while on his midterm blitz in September that hiked gas prices were a “very inexpensive price to pay for what we’ve done.”

“But that’s going to come tumbling down,” he added, referring to gas prices. “That’s going to be like rocket ships in reverse.”

The Fox News poll was conducted Oct 9 -12 among 1,202 registered voters. The margin of error was 2.5 percentage points.

articles.body:
President Trump said Wednesday night at a rally in Montana that he wasn’t sure who U.S. officials were negotiating with in their efforts to bring an end to the Iran war.

“They don’t have a navy. They don’t have an air force. Their army is decimated. Their leaders are gone,” the president said, referencing the state of the Iranian military while discussing the conflict. “I should have probably left their leaders because I don’t know who the hell we’re negotiating with.”

Trump arrived in the Treasure State Wednesday evening to campaign for Montana Republican Aaron Flint, who is vying to replace retiring Rep. Ryan Zinke (R-Mont.) and will face Democrat Sam Forstag in November.

The Iran war, which nears its eighth month, has put the GOP in tricky political territory heading into the midterm elections. The conflict has strained the global economy and raised fuel costs for Americans, who increasingly blame the president’s policies for rising prices.

But deliberations between the U.S. and Iran have stalled in recent weeks.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News’s Rachel Campos Duffy on Sunday , “I don’t know how this ends. You never know how this ends.”

Following unsuccessful talks at the United Nations General Assembly late last month, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the Iranian delegation “overstayed” its welcome and ordered its members to leave the U.S.

Vice President Vance said earlier this month that Iranian leadership must take serious steps to dismantle any pursuit of nuclear weapons.

“I think if they want to show a commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, they would do something meaningful on their enrichment capacity,” Vance told Reuters.

“In other words, the United States is not going to do things for mere promise of actions on the Iranian side. We need to trade actions for actions here, and we’ll see what the Iranians do,” he later added.
